paragraphs: Commercial microwave links can provide dense coverage for rainfall monitoring, but their measurements describe signal loss along an entire path. Recovering a rainfall map from those measurements therefore requires working backward from accumulated effects. Treating each link as a point sensor loses this spatial information, especially when rain varies substantially across the area.

The paper frames reconstruction as a Bayesian inverse problem: combine the measurements with a model of plausible rainfall fields. A diffusion model supplies that spatial prior, while the formulation accounts for the physical power-law relationship between rainfall and signal attenuation. The authors find that diffusion models preserve important rainfall statistics better than censored Gaussian processes.

This formulation supports training-free posterior sampling through several families of methods, including Plug-and-Play, Sequential Monte Carlo, and Replica Exchange. These methods produce rainfall fields informed by both the observations and the prior. Across synthetic and real-world datasets, the approach consistently improves on established microwave-link reconstruction baselines, supporting the value of combining realistic spatial structure with the measurement physics.
icml-2026-bayesian-rain-field-reconstruc.tldr: Diffusion-model priors improve rainfall reconstruction by combining realistic spatial patterns with the physics of microwave-link measurements.

paragraphs: Representing text as bytes allows a language model to accept any Unicode input, but it does not guarantee that generated bytes form valid text. A model can produce an invalid UTF-8 sequence, particularly around rare or unseen characters. This paper asks whether ordinary language-model evaluation captures the learning needed to avoid those structural errors.

The authors study a 355-million-parameter model trained on 80 billion tokens from a balanced English, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese corpus. They introduce evaluation protocols that separate UTF-8 structure from language prediction. In their experiments, perplexity stabilizes after 2.1 billion tokens, while UTF-8 validity takes 4.2 billion tokens to converge—roughly twice as much training.

The results also complicate the expectation that frequent characters should always be structurally easier. Without context, rare characters achieve higher validity than common ones, which the authors interpret as suggesting over-specialization of frequent-character representations. Together, these observations show that reliable encoding is a distinct learned capability in this setting. A stable perplexity score alone can therefore miss continued progress in producing well-formed text.
icml-2026-beyond-perplexity-utf-8-validi.tldr: UTF-8 generation reliability develops later than perplexity stabilizes, showing that byte-aware models need separate structural-validity evaluation.

paragraphs: Event-native spiking neural networks represent information through the timing and ordering of spikes. They operate directly on events rather than dividing time into fixed bins, allowing computation and memory to scale with the number of events. This matches the temporal representation of event sensors and neuromorphic hardware, but creates practical obstacles for training.

One obstacle is that charging, firing, and resetting a neuron appears to require processing input spikes sequentially. The authors use parallel associative scans to consume multiple input spikes together while preserving exact hard-reset dynamics. They report speedups of up to 44 times compared with sequential simulation, addressing a computational bottleneck without replacing those dynamics with an approximation.

The second obstacle is finding precise firing times in continuous time. The paper implements differentiable solvers that calculate spike times to machine precision without discrete time steps or restrictive analytic assumptions. Combining these solvers with parallel processing makes end-to-end training practical in the demonstrated settings. Experiments on four event-based datasets show that these temporally precise networks can be trained on GPUs.
icml-2026-bullet-trains-parallelizing-tr.tldr: Parallel spike processing and differentiable timing solvers make exact continuous-time spiking networks practical to train on GPUs.

paragraphs: Continual visual question answering often assigns a separate expert to each task and routes questions using task identity. This assumes the designated expert is the best source of an answer. The paper challenges that assumption: on the VQA-v2 task stream, an expert from another task performs better on 49.9% of queries.

The proposed system trains parameter-efficient adapters for individual tasks, then learns routing to directly maximize expected question-answering utility. At inference, Bayesian aggregation combines expert evidence within a shared answer space. An entropy penalty prevents routing from collapsing into a single-expert choice, allowing several plausible experts to contribute instead of discarding their transferable knowledge.

The method reports improved accuracy and reduced forgetting across three continual-learning settings. On VQA-v2 CL-LS, it achieves 64.16 accuracy and 0.63 forgetting, with reported improvements of 5.74 in accuracy and 2.99 less forgetting over the strongest prior method. Calibration also improves: expected calibration error falls from 0.15 to 0.07. These findings support pooling expert evidence while learning which contributions help answer each query.
icml-2026-calibrated-knowledge-aggregati.tldr: A calibrated Bayesian mixture combines knowledge across task experts to improve continual visual question answering and reduce forgetting.

paragraphs: A multi-step prompt injection can hide its harmful purpose across an agent’s workflow. Each individual action may look legitimate, while the full sequence produces an unwanted result. This creates a detection problem for defenses that inspect isolated inputs, outputs, or instruction patterns without representing how the actions depend on one another.

CausalTrace models those dependencies explicitly. It builds structural causal models from agent trajectories, distinguishing connections involving data dependencies, transfers of trust, and changes that enable later actions. It then uses causal intervention reasoning to ask whether the harmful outcome would have occurred if the injection had been blocked. That question helps distinguish injection-dependent attacks from benign workflows with similar surface features.

Evaluation covers crowdsourced traces, agent benchmarks, and semi-real and real scenarios. The system outperforms content-based baselines while requiring little LLM inference. Its bidirectional slicing procedure also reconstructs complete attack chains with high edge recall. The contribution is therefore both detection and explanation: the resulting chain links an observed harmful outcome back to the causal steps through which the injection enabled it.
icml-2026-causal-detection-of-multi-step.tldr: CausalTrace detects multi-step agent attacks by tracing whether a prompt injection causally enabled the harmful outcome.

paragraphs: Generative models need evidence about interacting factors to learn how those factors combine. In decentralized settings, relevant observations may be scattered across isolated data sources. A model that merely represents the union of those sources can capture what each contains while overlooking new combinations supported by their collective information.

Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching addresses that gap by enforcing structural constraints across the global set of generative factors. The framework uses interactions among peers without exchanging raw data. Its goal is to make compositions emerge from the distributed evidence even when no individual source contains enough information to support the composition independently.

The authors evaluate the framework on conditional image generation, robotic spatial planning, and medical attribute co-occurrence modeling. Across these settings, it substantially outperforms federated learning and mixture-of-experts baselines. The stated findings support a distinction between aggregating distributed observations and learning how their factors fit together. Here, peer interaction and global structural constraints provide a way to generate combinations that isolated sources cannot supply on their own.
icml-2026-compositional-generative-model.tldr: Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching learns novel factor combinations across data silos without exchanging raw data.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses a large training set into a small synthetic one while trying to preserve predictive performance. This paper shows that the compression can preserve useful information unevenly across demographic groups. When groups have different predictive patterns, a distilled dataset can lose signals that matter to particular subgroups and create substantial performance gaps.

The authors distinguish two sources of this problem: unequal group sizes and mismatched subgroup predictive patterns. Correcting the first does not eliminate the second, so balancing the dataset alone cannot resolve the demonstrated fairness gaps. Their formal analysis examines how these sources interact and motivates a shared target for the information retained during distillation.

That target is a barycenter: an aggregate representation of predictive information designed to be independent of group imbalance and to induce similar representations across subgroups. Distilling toward this shared representation can reduce fairness concerns while remaining compatible with existing distillation methods. Empirical results show substantial reductions in bias introduced by compression, supporting the importance of aligning predictive information as well as considering group counts.
icml-2026-fair-dataset-distillation-via-.tldr: Aligning subgroup predictive information during dataset distillation reduces fairness gaps that balancing group sizes alone does not remove.

paragraphs: Predicting future visual observations requires separating changes in the world from changes caused by the observer’s movement. Image-based world models can mix these effects, producing realistic-looking videos with inconsistent objects that morph or disappear. FR3D addresses this ambiguity by predicting a persistent three-dimensional latent representation of the evolving scene.

The approach explicitly separates scene evolution from the agent’s trajectory. It treats inferred ego-motion—the agent’s own movement—as a latent proxy for action, allowing future geometry to be modeled separately from viewpoint changes. This separation is the paper’s mechanism for resolving ambiguity between self-motion and world-motion and maintaining geometric consistency into the future.

FR3D also uses teacher-student distillation to transfer spatial knowledge from existing foundation models. The authors report that this supports robust zero-shot generalization. Experiments across multiple datasets show strong future dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular observations, including predictions two seconds ahead. The findings connect a persistent spatial representation with motion separation and transferred spatial knowledge, providing an approach to forecasting the changing world in three dimensions.
icml-2026-future-dynamic-3d-reconstructi.tldr: FR3D forecasts persistent 3D scenes by separating environmental motion from the agent’s own movement and distilling foundation-model spatial knowledge.

paragraphs: Measuring memorization is difficult because a model can know something about a training example through either dataset-specific information or general patterns. The paper introduces a method for estimating how much information a model contains about a datapoint and formally separates these two contributions. Unintended memorization concerns a particular dataset; generalization concerns the underlying process that generated it.

When generalization is completely eliminated, the authors can calculate total memorization and use it to estimate capacity. Their measurements put the capacity of the studied GPT-style models at approximately 3.6 bits per parameter. This is an empirical capacity estimate under that measurement setup, connecting model size with the amount of information retained.

The study trains hundreds of transformer language models, ranging from 500,000 to 1.5 billion parameters, on datasets of increasing size. Models initially memorize until their capacity fills; unintended memorization then decreases as generalization begins. The authors also derive scaling laws relating capacity and dataset size to membership inference. Together, the results describe how data volume changes the balance between retaining specific examples and learning broader structure.
icml-2026-how-much-can-language-models-m.tldr: Separating dataset-specific memorization from generalization yields an estimated capacity of about 3.6 bits per parameter in studied GPT-style models.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning produces representations from unlabeled data, but assessing their usefulness often requires training a supervised linear probe. That evaluation can be expensive and sensitive to hyperparameters. It also reveals relatively little about the geometry of the learned representation itself. IdEst explores whether a geometric measurement can provide a cheaper, informative assessment.

The method estimates intrinsic dimension using a minimum spanning tree dimension estimator. Intrinsic dimension describes the effective dimensional structure of the representations, giving a way to study how the learned data occupy their feature space. The paper motivates this choice through connections between intrinsic dimension and neural network generalization.

Across different datasets, architectures, and self-supervised objectives, IdEst strongly correlates with downstream linear-probe performance. The authors also demonstrate its use for hyperparameter selection, with substantially lower computational cost than supervised alternatives. These findings support intrinsic dimension as a useful proxy for representation quality. The proposed role is complementary to standard probing: it adds a geometric signal and a cheaper selection tool without claiming that correlation makes the two evaluations interchangeable.
icml-2026-idest-assessing-self-supervise.tldr: IdEst uses intrinsic dimension to assess self-supervised representations and select hyperparameters at lower cost than supervised probing.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings that approximate solutions to partial differential equations. A difficult case arises when boundary conditions vary greatly and strongly influence the solution. Information specified only on a boundary must affect predictions throughout the domain, and existing approaches can struggle to capture that dependence.

The paper handles boundary information by learning a latent pseudo-extension over the entire spatial domain. This turns boundary data into a form that standard operator-learning architectures can consume alongside ordinary domain inputs. Coupling the extension with a domain-to-domain neural operator lets the resulting model learn dependencies on both the interior inputs and complex, non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

To test this setting, the authors construct 18 datasets covering Poisson, linear elasticity, and hyperelasticity problems across diverse geometries. The boundary conditions include mixed types, component-specific constraints, and multiple segments. The approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with large improvements over baselines and no hyperparameter tuning across these datasets. These results support learned boundary extensions as a practical way to broaden the boundary conditions existing neural-operator frameworks can handle.
icml-2026-imposing-boundary-conditions-o.tldr: Learned extensions spread boundary information across a domain so standard neural operators can handle complex, highly variable boundary conditions.

paragraphs: Transformer Neural Processes perform well on tasks such as forecasting and tabular modeling, but streaming applications introduce a different requirement: updating predictions cheaply whenever an observation arrives. Existing variants recompute internal representations rather than incrementally extending them. This makes repeated updates expensive for applications involving continuous sensor readings or database changes.

The proposed Incremental Transformer Neural Process combines causal masking, key-value caching, and a data-efficient autoregressive training strategy. Together, these allow the model to reuse previous computations and reduce update complexity from quadratic to linear. Experiments on synthetic and real-world tasks, including tabular regression and temperature prediction, show comparable or better predictive performance than non-causal alternatives and orders-of-magnitude faster sequential inference.

The authors also examine whether incremental processing compromises the consistency of prediction updates. Using an adapted measure of implicit Bayesianness, they find that the model is as implicitly Bayesian as standard non-causal Transformer Neural Processes under a one-at-a-time streaming protocol. This qualified result supports the approach’s ability to combine cheaper sequential updates with the measured consistency needed for streaming inference.
icml-2026-incremental-transformer-neural.tldr: Incremental Transformer Neural Processes reuse cached computation to accelerate streaming updates while preserving predictive performance and measured update consistency.

paragraphs: A language model’s key-value cache stores information from earlier tokens for use during subsequent generation. As context grows, this cache becomes a major memory cost. Existing eviction methods often decide what to retain using recency or previous attention scores, which provide indirect evidence about whether a token will matter later.

KV Policy instead learns to rank cached tokens by predicted future usefulness. It trains lightweight reinforcement-learning agents for individual attention heads using precomputed generation traces and only key and value vectors. A reward based on future utility evaluates the entire ranking across cache budgets, encouraging policies that support different amounts of available memory without modifying the underlying language model.

Across two model families, the method significantly outperforms strong baselines on RULER contexts up to 128,000 tokens and on the OASST2-4k dialogue benchmark. Zero-shot evaluations on BoolQ, LongBench passage retrieval, and GovReport also show transfer beyond the training distribution and to substantially longer sequences. The results support learning future utility directly as a practical basis for deciding which cached information to discard.
icml-2026-learning-to-evict-from-key-val.tldr: KV Policy learns attention-head-specific eviction rankings that predict which cached tokens will help future generation.

paragraphs: A model may solve individual reasoning steps successfully yet struggle to manage a long sequence of dependent steps. LongCoT is designed to measure that extended reasoning capability directly. It contains 2,500 expert-designed problems spanning chemistry, mathematics, computer science, chess, and logic, with short inputs and answers that can be verified.

The difficulty comes from navigating a graph of interdependent reasoning steps. Solving the problems requires reasoning traces ranging from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens, even though each local step is individually tractable for frontier models. This design makes long-horizon coordination central to the evaluation rather than relying on a single unusually difficult operation.

At the benchmark’s release, the best reported models remain below 10% accuracy: GPT 5.2 reaches 9.8%, and Gemini 3 Pro reaches 6.1%. These results expose a substantial gap between handling local steps and sustaining reliable reasoning across a much larger dependency structure. The benchmark provides a scalable way to track improvements in planning and managing such extended reasoning processes.
icml-2026-longcot-benchmarking-long-hori.tldr: LongCoT exposes major failures in sustained reasoning through problems whose manageable individual steps form very long dependency chains.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised imitation learning combines a small collection of trajectories with action labels and a much larger collection without them. An inverse dynamics model predicts which action connects a current state to the next state. It can supply missing labels for behavior cloning or work alongside a video model to produce a policy.

The authors show that these two uses learn the same policy in a limiting case. They then argue that previously observed advantages over behavior cloning arise from the sample efficiency of learning inverse dynamics. Their explanation has two parts: the true inverse dynamics model tends to belong to a less complex hypothesis class, and it is often less stochastic than the expert policy.

The argument combines statistical learning insights with new experiments, including models for unified video-action prediction. It also motivates an improved version of LAPO for learning latent action policies. Experiments use Procgen, Push-T, and LIBERO. The paper thus connects different inverse-dynamics approaches through a common limiting policy and explains why inferring actions from state transitions can require fewer labeled examples.
icml-2026-on-the-sample-efficiency-of-in.tldr: Inverse dynamics can make imitation learning more sample-efficient because predicting actions from transitions may be simpler and less stochastic than learning the expert policy.

paragraphs: An ensemble runs several neural networks to gain predictive performance, but that benefit comes with additional computation. Combining their weights into a single aggregate model reduces cost while typically sacrificing accuracy. Partial fusion introduces intermediate choices, allowing some neurons to be merged while others remain separate.

The guiding principle is similarity: neurons that behave most similarly across networks are candidates for aggregation. The authors present a method based on partial optimal transport that jointly identifies these similarities and matches the neurons to merge. This provides a way to adjust the balance between keeping the ensemble’s distinct components and reducing repeated computation through shared components.

The paper also interprets partial fusion as a broader form of pruning. Under this view, neurons can be deleted or linearly combined, expanding the available operations beyond removal alone. Applying this generalized pruning to a single network produces similar benefits, with tradeoffs among retaining separate neurons, deleting them, and combining them according to similarity. The contribution is a flexible framework connecting ensemble compression, weight aggregation, and network pruning.
icml-2026-partial-fusion-of-neural-netwo.tldr: Partial fusion merges similar neurons while retaining others, creating flexible efficiency–performance tradeoffs between full ensembles and weight aggregation.

paragraphs: Finding antimicrobial peptides requires searching an enormous space in which active candidates are relatively scarce. Generative models offer latent representations for navigating that space, but ordinary flat distances can distort exploration by ignoring how the decoder transforms latent changes into peptides. The paper also challenges manifold approaches that assume a fixed intrinsic dimension.

PepCompass represents the space as a union of κ-stable Riemannian manifolds, capturing local decoder geometry while maintaining computational stability. For global exploration, Potential-minimizing Geodesic Search guides interpolation toward promising seeds. For local refinement, the framework combines geometry-aware Brownian sampling with mutation enumeration in tangent space, forming a procedure called Local Enumeration Bayesian Optimization.

The reported discovery process identifies four novel seeds and optimizes them into 25 highly active, broad-spectrum peptides. The authors report a 100% in-vitro validation rate for their results. This demonstrates the value of geometry-informed exploration in the study’s peptide discovery setting: the global search finds promising starting points, and the local procedure refines them while accounting for the structure induced by the decoder.
icml-2026-pepcompass-navigating-peptide-.tldr: PepCompass uses decoder-aware geometry to discover and refine antimicrobial peptides, reporting 25 highly active candidates and 100% in-vitro validation.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy-gradient post-training in linear autoregressive models whose target sequences satisfy a margin condition. That condition extends separability to sequences and underpins the theoretical guarantees. The central question is how reward feedback can improve correct-response likelihood, especially when the base model initially assigns little probability to the desired response.

For test samples with non-trivial base likelihood α, a policy-gradient variant can reach likelihood 1 − ε using an essentially minimax-optimal number of reward queries, scaling roughly as (α⁻¹ + ε⁻¹)/γ² up to logarithmic factors. However, outcome rewards face a base-model barrier. Overall expected error depends on a property called the Likelihood Quantile, and moving beyond the base model’s support may require exponentially many queries in sequence length.

The authors then analyze process rewards, which provide feedback within the sequence. Their policy-gradient variants avoid that sequence-length curse through dependence on a token-level Likelihood Quantile. Additional results establish near-optimal statistical-learning error and online mistake guarantees with adaptive learning rates under the margin condition. The findings explain both the strength and the conditional limits of post-training from final-outcome feedback.
icml-2026-post-training-with-policy-grad.tldr: For linear autoregressive models under a margin condition, policy gradients are nearly optimal but outcome rewards can face an exponential base-model barrier.

paragraphs: Interpolating between generated samples can reveal how a model organizes its learned distribution, but ordinary latent-space interpolation may pass through low-density regions. This paper adapts the string method to evolve entire curves under a diffusion model’s learned score function. The method works with pretrained models and requires no retraining.

Different settings of the framework produce different kinds of paths. Generative transport yields continuous sample trajectories; gradient-dominated dynamics recover minimum-energy paths; and finite-temperature dynamics produce principal curves that balance energy and entropy. In image experiments, this distinction matters: minimum-energy paths include high-likelihood but unrealistic cartoon-like images, whereas principal curves produce realistic morphing sequences despite having lower likelihood.

The authors also apply the method to protein structure prediction. Models trained on static structures yield transition pathways between metastable conformations with physically plausible intermediate structures. These findings support the string method as a tool for examining how learned modes connect and what barriers separate them. They also show why choosing a path solely for high likelihood can give a different picture from choosing one that reflects realistic variation.
icml-2026-probing-the-geometry-of-diffus.tldr: The string method maps paths through pretrained diffusion models, revealing how realistic transitions can differ from high-likelihood paths.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization trains policies using groups of sampled responses and their rewards. This paper analyzes the case of verifiable binary rewards, where each response succeeds or fails. It shows that normalizing rewards by their mean and variance induces a contrastive loss whose comparison examples are generated by the previous policy.

The authors study variants with mean-only or mean-and-variance normalization and different forms of KL regularization. Updates may be constrained toward the previous policy, a fixed reference policy, or both. For each analyzed variant, they derive an explicit optimal policy using the rewards, their statistics under the previous policy, and the relevant previous and reference policies.

This explicit characterization turns repeated optimization into a simple recurrence for the probability of success. The recurrence converges to a fixed point determined by the reference policy’s success probability and the regularization strength. The authors show that this fixed point improves on the reference. The analysis therefore explains success amplification within these variants and makes the influence of reward normalization and regularization on their dynamics mathematically explicit.
icml-2026-reinforcement-learning-with-ve.tldr: An analysis of GRPO variants derives explicit policy updates and shows how their success probabilities converge above the reference policy’s.

paragraphs: Language-model safety mechanisms must recognize harmful meaning even when the presentation of text changes. This paper investigates weaknesses involving spatially structured text perturbations. The authors connect those weaknesses to token-by-token autoregressive generation and argue that current semantic representations are insufficiently robust to this kind of spatial variation.

SpatialJB is an attack framework that exploits this weakness to alter output generation and allow harmful content to pass output guardrails. The contribution centers on spatial semantics: the relationship between meaning and how text is arranged. This extends the evaluation of guardrails beyond whether they recognize harmful content in its ordinary presentation.

Across the leading language models tested, the authors report an attack success rate approaching 100%. They also report success above 75% against advanced output guardrails, including the OpenAI Moderation API, and substantial improvements over existing jailbreak techniques. These are experimental findings for the evaluated settings. The paper additionally proposes and evaluates baseline defenses, pairing the vulnerability analysis with attempts to prevent misuse and improve robustness to spatially structured perturbations.
icml-2026-spatialjb-how-text-distributio.tldr: SpatialJB exposes experimentally strong jailbreak vulnerabilities involving spatial text structure and evaluates baseline defenses against them.

paragraphs: Controlling diffusion generation requires guidance that remains useful as noise changes the available information. The paper argues that only a small number of features remain informative for control as data become increasingly corrupted. Spectral Guidance identifies those features through the geometry of the generative process rather than treating every possible signal as equally useful.

The authors characterize the features as singular functions of a conditional expectation operator and learn them through a self-supervised objective. Once learned, this basis projects guidance such as labels, CLIP embeddings, or masks onto the sampling trajectory. Sampling then supports stable, high-fidelity control without retraining or backpropagating through the denoiser, and the same representations support spatial guidance without auxiliary models.

On CIFAR-10, the method improves conditional accuracy by 37 percentage points over the strongest training-free baseline while sampling four times faster. The framework also reveals a phase transition that identifies an optimal window for applying guidance. Together, these findings connect efficient control with both which features survive noise and when those features can most effectively influence generation.
icml-2026-spectral-guidance-for-flexible.tldr: Spectral Guidance learns noise-relevant features that enable flexible diffusion control with faster sampling and no denoiser backpropagation during sampling.

paragraphs: Preference optimization can teach a model to rely on features correlated with preferred answers without those features being the reason the answers are better. Such shortcuts contribute to behaviors including sycophancy and length bias. This paper provides a theoretical account of how that reliance develops and why collecting more similar preference data may fail to remove it.

For log-linear policies, the authors identify two population-level mechanisms: mean spurious bias and leakage from correlations between causal and spurious features. Because these mechanisms belong to the training distribution itself, additional data from that same distribution do not eliminate the resulting dependence. That dependence creates a persistent vulnerability when deployment conditions change.

The proposed mitigation, tie training, augments the data with preference pairs of equal utility. These ties introduce data-driven regularization that selectively reduces spurious learning without degrading causal learning in the analysis. Experiments validate the theory for log-linear models and provide evidence that the mechanisms and benefits also persist in neural networks and large language models. The work connects a formal diagnosis with a targeted change to preference data.
icml-2026-spurious-correlation-learning-.tldr: Tie training uses equal-utility preference pairs to reduce spurious feature learning that more data from the same distribution cannot eliminate.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be expensive to deploy, and different parts of the model present different compression challenges. Structured weight pruning may require lengthy retraining, while token compression introduces dependencies between layers that complicate optimization. ToaSt addresses these issues with separate strategies for attention modules and feed-forward networks.

For multi-head self-attention, ToaSt uses coupled head-wise structured pruning designed around the attention operation. For feed-forward networks, which account for more than 60% of floating-point operations in the paper’s framing, it introduces Token Channel Selection. This component filters redundant noise channels during inference without training, targeting a major source of computation.

Evaluations across nine models, including DeiT, ViT-MAE, and Swin Transformer, show better accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs than the tested baselines. On ViT-MAE-Huge, ToaSt reaches 88.52% accuracy, an increase of 1.64 percentage points, while reducing floating-point operations by 39.4%. It also transfers to detection, segmentation, and classification tasks, including COCO detection performance of 52.2 versus 51.9 mAP. The findings support tailoring compression to each component’s computational role.
icml-2026-toast-token-channel-selection-.tldr: ToaSt combines attention pruning with training-free feed-forward channel selection to improve Vision Transformer accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Adaptive computation aims to spend more inference effort on difficult tokens and less on easy ones. But natural-language task scores do not directly reveal each token’s difficulty, making it hard to tell whether extra computation follows genuine complexity. Architectural differences can further obscure what the allocation mechanism itself contributes.

The paper introduces a controlled evaluation using algorithmic and synthetic language tasks with adjustable difficulty. It also presents ANIRA, a recurrent Transformer framework that supports variable computation depth for each token while separating allocation decisions from other model factors. This setup lets the authors examine complexity alignment, generalization, and the timing of decisions within a common framework.

The experiments show that computation can align with task complexity without explicit difficulty supervision. However, that alignment does not establish algorithmic generalization: models still fail on unseen input sizes despite spending additional computation. The authors also find that early allocation decisions rely on static structural cues, while online stopping decisions track algorithmic execution state more closely. These results distinguish learning where to spend effort from learning procedures that extrapolate.
icml-2026-understanding-dynamic-compute-.tldr: Controlled experiments show that recurrent Transformers can allocate compute according to difficulty without learning to generalize to larger unseen problems.
